title: Social protection is becoming the political infrastructure of climate adaptation, but coverage gaps leave children, workers and informal livelihoods exposed
source_unit: International Labour Organization, World Social Protection Report 2024–2026: Universal Social Protection for Climate Action and a Just Transition
geography: Global coverage and financing estimates with regional and income-group comparisons

denominator.unit: Global population and population-group estimates under SDG indicator 1.3.1; coverage means effective access to at least one social-protection benefit

at_least_one_benefit_2023.unit: percent of the world’s population covered by at least one social-protection benefit in 2023

at_least_one_benefit_2015.unit: percent of the world’s population covered by at least one social-protection benefit in 2015

coverage_trajectory.value: High-income countries approach universal coverage while low-income-country coverage remains 9.7%

observations.method: ILO global and regional social-protection estimates based on SDG indicator 1.3.1 and the World Social Protection Database.
observations.uncertainty: Coverage indicates receipt or effective access to at least one benefit, not adequacy, duration, portability, service quality or protection from all life-cycle risks.
observations.subgroup: Global population, income groups and population groups covered by social-protection benefits.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coverage expansion is meaningful progress, but aggregate improvement can coexist with severe gaps for specific workers, children, women and climate-exposed populations.

denominator.unit: Global children, workers and working-age populations; each measure uses its stated ILO coverage denominator

children_with_benefit.unit: percent of children aged 0–18 receiving a family or child benefit

children_uncovered.unit: children aged 0–18 without a family or child benefit

sickness_legal_coverage.unit: percent of the global labor force legally entitled to sickness benefits

employment_injury_protection.unit: percent of workers with employment-injury protection

unemployment_benefit_coverage.unit: percent of unemployed people receiving unemployment cash benefits

observations.method: ILO life-course social-protection coverage estimates for children and working-age people.
observations.uncertainty: Legal entitlement, effective receipt and benefit adequacy are different concepts; global aggregates conceal major regional, gender, sector and employment-status differences.
observations.subgroup: Children, workers, people experiencing sickness or work injury, and unemployed people.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low coverage may reflect informal employment, administrative barriers, eligibility rules or benefit design rather than only low public spending.

denominator.unit: Countries and aggregate GDP estimates; expenditure excludes healthcare unless otherwise stated

low_middle_income_financing_gap.unit: additional annual US dollars low- and middle-income countries require to guarantee at least a basic social-protection floor

financing_gap_gdp.unit: percent of aggregate GDP in low- and middle-income countries represented by the annual social-protection financing gap

working_age_social_protection_spending.unit: percent of global GDP allocated to non-health public social-protection expenditure for working-age people

income_group_spending_gap.value: Working-age social-protection expenditure averages 6.3% of GDP in high-income countries and 0.4% in low-income countries

observations.method: ILO social-protection financing and expenditure estimates with income-group comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Financing needs are modeled estimates and depend on benefit floors, health-system costs, administrative capacity, fiscal space, demographics and national policy choices.
observations.subgroup: Low- and middle-income countries, high-income and low-income country groups, and working-age populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: More spending is not sufficient without effective administration, inclusive eligibility, social dialogue and benefits that are adequate relative to living costs and shocks.

observations.period: 2024–2026; social protection as climate and just-transition infrastructure

denominator.unit: Global and country systems; policy synthesis rather than a single statistical denominator

climate_coverage_vulnerability.unit: percent of the population effectively covered in the 50 countries most vulnerable to climate change

climate_exposure_unprotected.unit: people in the 50 most climate-vulnerable countries facing intensifying livelihood, income and health impacts without social protection

transition_policy.value: Social protection should be coordinated with skills, active labor-market policies, health, income security and climate policy to make decarbonization politically and socially sustainable

state_trust.value: Stronger social protection can reinforce the social contract, state-society trust and willingness to accept climate policies

observations.method: ILO policy analysis linking social protection, climate adaptation, mitigation and just-transition labor-market change.
observations.uncertainty: The report establishes a policy mechanism and coverage risk, not a causal estimate of how much social protection increases climate-policy support in each country.
observations.subgroup: Climate-vulnerable populations, workers in transitioning sectors, informal workers, children, women and households facing shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social protection can build legitimacy only when benefits are accessible, visibly fair and financed in ways that do not shift costs onto already exposed households.

related_sources.claim: Official ILO World Social Protection Report 2024–2026 PDF used for retrieval verification and hashing.
Official ILO chapter on social protection’s role in climate adaptation and a just transition.

boundary: This record adds a protection-to-legitimacy mechanism: social protection is not only a poverty instrument but infrastructure for household resilience, labor-market transitions and politically sustainable climate action. It is an ILO global statistical and policy report, not a household panel, causal evaluation of benefits or country-specific implementation audit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO report landing page, executive summary, chapters on climate and life-course protection, and report PDF were retrieved and reviewed for coverage, child and working-age protection, financing gaps, unemployment protection and just-transition legitimacy; the PDF was hashed.
